newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden OM Group head supports common Nordic system.
newsitem.headline: Sweden OM Group head supports common Nordic system.

text.p: Per Larsson, head of Swedish futures and options exchange OM Group told Reuters on Monday the idea of a common Nordic transaction network was appealing.
But he said a pan-Nordic exchange was unlikely despite several cross-border links in the past few months.
"We believe in a common Nordic transaction network. We would like to offer Nordic shares and products to our customers, but a joint exchange is not necessary for that," Larsson said.
"I don't believe in a Nordic bourse. There are too many advantages that local bourses have for it to be a good idea, such as being in contact with the companies," he said.

The Helsinki Stock Exchange and Finnish derivatives exchange SOM Oy said last week they would merge and create a new company called HEX Oy by year-end. They said the merger was aimed at simplifying their structures and boosting competitiveness.
Last month, the Copenhagen and Stockholm bourses said they would combine their trading systems and last year, Denmark's stock and futures and options exchanges said they would link up.
In February, OM opened a real-time link with the Oslo bourse so Norwegian and Swedish derivatives could trade in a single system.

"We are also interested in offering our customers Norwegian shares, but we...decided to wait until they decided which trading system they would chose," he said. "Now that they have chosen an Australian trading system, it is time to take up discussion."
But OM sees a link to Danish markets less likely.
"It would be difficult to make such an investment profitable. Turnover on the Danish market is still too small," OM spokesman Gustaf Sahlman said.
Larsson said a quick deal with Sweden's stock exchange and OM was necessary in order not to lose the advantages of a merger. Both sides were awaiting the results from a third-party investigation.
"If talks do not start up again in the autumn, and we develop in a different direction than the stock exchange, I think some of the advantages of a merger could be lost," Larsson said.
He said a merger was essential because "a simple link between the two exchanges does not give the synergies that we would have if a merger took place."
"We would like to be able to supply Swedish shares to our customers, and if a merger doesn't take place, cooperation is another, although less desireable, alternative," he said.
